places.name: Pergamum

status.t: bequeathed to Rome by Attalus III

places.summary: Attalid capital whose last king, Attalus III, left his kingdom to Rome in 133 BC, creating the province of Asia after Aristonicus's revolt (133-129). Its library rivalled Alexandria's; Galen was born here (129).

places.name: Ephesus

status.t: seat of the proconsul of Asia

places.summary: Seat of the proconsul of Asia and its greatest city, with the temple of Artemis. Mithridates ordered the massacre of 80,000 Romans and Italians in Asia from here in 88 BC. The councils of 431 and 449 (the 'Robber Synod') met here.

places.name: Smyrna

status.t: won the right to a temple of Tiberius
rebuilt after earthquake by Marcus Aurelius

places.summary: Ionian port that won the competition to build Asia's temple to Tiberius, Livia and the Senate (AD 26). Polycarp was martyred in its stadium (c. 155-167).

places.name: Sardis

status.t: destroyed by earthquake, rebuilt with imperial aid

places.summary: Lydian royal city and Persian satrapal capital, western end of the Royal Road. Ruined by the great earthquake of 17 and rebuilt with Tiberius's remission of tribute; its huge synagogue (3rd-4th century) is the largest known in the diaspora.

places.name: Miletus
places.summary: Ionian port, mother of Black Sea colonies. Young Caesar was captured by pirates near it c. 75 BC and later crucified them. The market gate is in Berlin.

places.name: Didyma

status.t: oracle consulted by Diocletian before the persecution

places.summary: Oracle of Apollo Didymaeus whose colossal temple was never finished. Diocletian consulted it in 303, and its reply (Lactantius, Mort. Pers. 11) was taken as approval for the Great Persecution.

places.name: Magnesia ad Sipylum
places.summary: City in the Hermus valley near which L. Cornelius Scipio and Eumenes II defeated Antiochus III in winter 190/189 BC, leading to the Peace of Apamea.

places.name: Aphrodisias
places.summary: Carian city of Aphrodite favoured by Caesar and Octavian; its archive wall copies Roman letters granting freedom. The Sebasteion reliefs show Claudius subduing Britannia; its marble school supplied the empire.

places.name: Laodicea ad Lycum

status.t: rebuilt after earthquake from own funds

places.summary: Wealthy Phrygian city that refused imperial aid after the earthquake of 60 (Tac. Ann. 14.27). Cicero held court here as governor of Cilicia (51-50 BC).

places.name: Hierapolis
places.summary: Spa city above the travertine terraces of Pamukkale, with the Plutonium cave of poisonous gas Strabo tested with sparrows (13.4.14). A 3rd-century relief there depicts the earliest known crank-and-rod sawmill.

places.name: Apamea Kibotos
places.summary: Phrygian city where the Peace of Apamea (188 BC) confined Antiochus III beyond the Taurus, fined him 15,000 talents and handed his ships and elephants to Rome.

places.name: Ilium
places.foundedNote: Hellenistic polis on the site of Troy
places.summary: Troy, which Rome honoured as the mother city of Aeneas; Fimbria sacked it in 85 BC and Caesar and Augustus restored it. Constantine reportedly considered it for his new capital.

places.name: Cyzicus
places.summary: Island city on the Propontis besieged by Mithridates VI in 73 BC; Lucullus starved the royal army into retreat. Its Hadrianic temple was a wonder of the world for later writers.

places.name: Nicomedia
places.summary: Bithynian royal capital, then Diocletian's main residence, where the edict of the Great Persecution was posted on 24 February 303 and Diocletian abdicated on 1 May 305. Pliny the Younger reported a fire here and asked to found a fire brigade, refused by Trajan (Ep. 10.33-34). Constantine died nearby in 337.

places.name: Nicaea
places.summary: Bithynian city whose walls survive almost complete. Constantine's council of May-July 325 condemned Arius and fixed the Nicene creed.

places.name: Chalcedon
places.summary: Megarian colony facing Byzantium. The council of 451 defined Christ in two natures, splitting the Miaphysite churches of Egypt and Syria from the imperial church. Shahin's Persian army watched the siege of 626 from here.

places.name: Sinope
places.summary: Milesian port and capital of Mithridates VI, who was born here; Lucullus took it in 70 BC. Caesar planted a colony. Birthplace of Diogenes the Cynic and of the heretic Marcion.

places.name: Trapezus
places.summary: Black Sea port where Xenophon's Ten Thousand reached the sea. Hadrian built its harbour; Arrian's Periplus (131) starts here. Gothic seaborne raiders sacked it in 257 despite its garrison.

places.name: Ancyra
places.foundedNote: Galatian Tectosages town; capital of Galatia 25 BC
places.summary: Capital of Galatia, whose temple of Rome and Augustus carries the best copy of the Res Gestae Divi Augusti in Latin and Greek, the 'Monumentum Ancyranum'.

places.name: Pessinus
places.summary: Temple-state of the Great Mother, whose black stone was brought to Rome in 204 BC on Sibylline advice during the Hannibalic war, welcomed by Scipio Nasica as the 'best man' in Rome.

places.name: Caesarea Mazaca

status.t: capital of the province of Cappadocia

places.summary: Cappadocian capital renamed Caesarea by Archelaus, annexed by Tiberius in 17. Shapur I took it in 260 after a long siege; Basil the Great was its bishop (370-379).

places.name: Tarsus
places.summary: Capital of Cilicia, where Cleopatra sailed up the Cydnus to meet Antony in 41 BC. Birthplace of Paul. Julian was buried here in 363; Maximinus Daia died here in 313.

places.name: Side
places.summary: Pamphylian port off which the Rhodian fleet, with Hannibal commanding a Seleucid squadron, fought in 190 BC; Hannibal was defeated (Livy 37.23-24).

places.name: Perge
places.summary: Pamphylian city on the Via Sebaste; its benefactress Plancia Magna (c. 120) rebuilt the gate with statues of the city's founders and imperial family.

places.name: Iconium
places.summary: Lycaonian city on the Via Sebaste visited by Paul and Barnabas; Augustus planted a colony beside the Greek city.

places.name: Antiochia Pisidiae
places.summary: Augustan colony and military base for the Homonadensian war, hub of the Via Sebaste. A Latin copy of the Res Gestae was set up here.

places.name: Zela
places.summary: Pontic temple town where Caesar crushed Pharnaces II in a five-day campaign on 2 August 47 BC and wrote 'veni, vidi, vici'.

places.name: Satala
places.summary: Fortress guarding the route into Armenia. Galerius won his decisive victory over Narseh in Armenia from here in 298; Justinian rebuilt its walls.

places.name: Melitene
places.summary: Fortress of XII Fulminata near a crossing of the Euphrates; Khosrow I was defeated near here in 576 and nearly drowned crossing the river.

places.name: Samosata
places.modern: Samsat (flooded by the Atatürk Dam), Turkey
places.summary: Commagenian royal capital annexed in 72, birthplace of Lucian. Its mound now lies under the waters of the Atatürk reservoir.

places.name: Nisibis
places.summary: Bastion of Roman Mesopotamia, besieged three times by Shapur II (337, 346, 350), once with a dammed river. Its surrender by Jovian in 363 was a national trauma; Ephrem the Syrian left with its Christians for Edessa.

places.name: Amida
places.summary: Fortress-city on the Tigris whose fall to Shapur II after a 73-day siege in 359 is narrated by Ammianus, who escaped from it. Kavad I took it again in 503 after a three-month siege.

places.name: Dara
places.summary: Fortress city built by Anastasius after the war of 502-506 to face Nisibis, against treaty terms. Belisarius defeated a larger Persian army outside its walls in 530 using trenches; its fall in 573 drove Justin II mad.

places.name: Edessa
places.summary: Capital of the Abgarid kings of Osroene and heartland of Syriac Christianity, whose legend of Jesus's letter to Abgar and the Mandylion image was believed to protect it from Persian sieges.

places.name: Carrhae
places.summary: City of the moon god Sin near which the Parthian general Surena destroyed Crassus's army in June 53 BC, capturing seven eagles. Caracalla was murdered on the road from Edessa to its temple in April 217.

places.name: Theodosiopolis
places.summary: Armenian Karin, fortified under Theodosius II after the partition of Armenia (c. 387) as the main Roman bastion facing Persarmenia.

places.name: Rhesaena

status.t: Gordian III defeats Shapur I nearby

places.summary: Town at the Khabur springs where Gordian III's army defeated Shapur I in 243; its colonial coinage shows the standard of III Parthica.

places.name: Singara
places.foundedNote: colonia and fortress of I Parthica
places.summary: Severan fortress under the Jebel Sinjar. Constantius II's army fought a confused night battle near it in 344; Shapur II took it in 360 and deported its garrison.

places.name: Hatra
places.foundedNote: Arab caravan city and sanctuary of the Sun god
places.summary: Desert city of the Arab kings of Araba, which repelled Trajan (117) and Septimius Severus twice (198-199) before accepting a Roman garrison c. 235; Shapur I destroyed it c. 240. ISIS damaged its temples in 2015.

places.name: Dura-Europos
places.summary: Euphrates town sealed by Shapur I's siege in 256, preserving a painted synagogue, the earliest dated house-church, a Mithraeum, papyri of the cohors XX Palmyrenorum and mines where Persians apparently gassed Roman counter-miners with sulphur and bitumen.

places.name: Ctesiphon
places.summary: Parthian and Sasanian capital on the Tigris, taken by Trajan (116), Avidius Cassius (165), Severus (198) and Carus (283). Julian won a battle before its walls in 363 but could not take it. Its vaulted Taq Kasra hall survives.

places.name: Seleucia on the Tigris
places.foundedNote: founded c. 305 BC by Seleucus I
places.summary: Seleucus's eastern capital, a Greek city of perhaps 600,000 (Pliny). Its sack by Avidius Cassius in 165 was blamed for spreading the Antonine plague.

places.name: Artaxata
places.foundedNote: founded by Artaxias I c. 176 BC (Hannibal said to have advised)
places.summary: Armenian royal capital that Plutarch says Hannibal planned for King Artaxias. Corbulo burned it in 58; Statius Priscus took it in 163 and built a new capital (Kainepolis).

places.name: Phasis
places.summary: Greek port at the mouth of the Rioni with a Roman fort Arrian inspected in 131. In the Lazic War (541-562) its siege by the Persians in 556 was repulsed.

places.name: Pityus
places.summary: The most distant Roman fort on the eastern Black Sea, repulsing Gothic seaborne attacks c. 254 before falling c. 258 (Zosimus 1.32-33).

places.name: Antiochia
places.summary: Seleucid capital on the Orontes, third city of the empire, and residence of emperors campaigning in the East. The disciples were first called Christians here. Sacked by Shapur I (253 or 256) and Khosrow I (540), and devastated by the earthquakes of 115, 526 and 528.

places.name: Seleucia Pieria
places.summary: Antioch's port and base of the Classis Syriaca; Vespasian and Titus cut the 1.4 km Titus tunnel to divert floods away from it.

places.name: Apamea
places.summary: Seleucid elephant base with a 2 km colonnaded street. Legion II Parthica wintered here in 215-218 and 231-233 (tombstones in the city wall).

places.name: Laodicea ad Mare
places.summary: Seleucid port rewarded by Septimius Severus with colonial status and temporary primacy over Antioch, which had backed Pescennius Niger.

places.name: Emesa
places.summary: Seat of the dynasty of priest-kings of the sun god Elagabal, which produced Julia Domna and the emperors Elagabalus and Severus Alexander. Aurelian defeated Zenobia's army here in 272.

places.name: Palmyra
places.summary: Caravan city whose merchants ran the trade from the Persian Gulf. Odaenathus avenged Valerian's capture; his widow Zenobia seized Egypt and Asia Minor (270-272) until Aurelian took the city twice. Its temple of Bel was blown up by ISIS in 2015.

places.name: Damascus
places.summary: Oasis city, Nabataean for a time under Aretas IV (when Paul escaped in a basket). Its surrender to Khalid ibn al-Walid in 635 and the battle of the Yarmuk (636) ended Roman Syria.

places.name: Heliopolis
places.foundedNote: part of the colony of Berytus; separate colony under Severus
places.summary: Sanctuary of Jupiter Heliopolitanus with the largest Roman temple ever built, on a podium including the 800-tonne trilithon blocks. Constantine and Theodosius suppressed its cults.

places.name: Berytus
places.foundedNote: Colonia Iulia Augusta Felix Berytus c. 15 BC (Agrippa)

status.t: veteran colony of V Macedonica and VIII Augusta

places.summary: Augustan veteran colony, a Latin island in the Greek East, which became the empire's leading law school (Ulpian and Papinian are linked to it) until the earthquake of 9 July 551.

places.name: Tyrus
places.summary: Phoenician island city, joined to the mainland by Alexander's mole, famed for purple dye. Origen died here c. 253. Its hippodrome is one of the largest known.

places.name: Sidon
places.summary: Phoenician city of glass and purple, a colonia under Elagabalus.

places.name: Caesarea Maritima
places.foundedNote: built by Herod 22-10/9 BC on Strato's Tower

status.t: seat of the prefect of Judaea

places.summary: Herod's harbour city with Sebastos, an artificial port built with hydraulic concrete from Puteoli. Seat of the governors of Judaea; the Pilate stone (1961) names Pontius Pilate as prefect. Origen and Eusebius worked in its library.

places.name: Hierosolyma
places.foundedNote: Jebusite and Israelite city; capital of Judaea
places.summary: Temple city taken by Pompey in 63 BC (he entered the Holy of Holies) and destroyed by Titus after a five-month siege in 70. Hadrian refounded it as Aelia Capitolina, a cause of the Bar Kokhba revolt. Constantine built the Holy Sepulchre; Khosrow II's army took the True Cross in 614, restored by Heraclius in 630.

places.name: Masada
places.summary: Herod's palace-fortress above the Dead Sea, last stronghold of the Sicarii. X Fretensis besieged it from eight camps and built a ramp; Josephus says the 960 defenders killed themselves before the assault (BJ 7.389-401).

places.name: Scythopolis
places.summary: Decapolis city west of the Jordan, capital of Palaestina Secunda, whose colonnaded streets were thrown down by the earthquake of 749.

places.name: Gerasa
places.summary: Decapolis city with an oval forum and an arch for Hadrian's visit of 129-130; its 6th-century churches have mosaics depicting Alexandria and Memphis.

places.name: Philadelphia
places.foundedNote: Ammonite Rabbath Ammon refounded by Ptolemy II
places.summary: Decapolis city on the Via Nova Traiana with a theatre for 6,000; Ptolemy II renamed Rabbath Ammon after himself.

places.name: Bostra
places.summary: Nabataean city made capital of Arabia in 106 and base of III Cyrenaica; start of the Via Nova Traiana. Its basalt theatre survives inside an Ayyubid castle.

places.name: Petra
places.summary: Rock-cut Nabataean capital annexed with the kingdom in 106; Hadrian visited in 130 and renamed it Hadriane. The Petra papyri (6th century), carbonised in a church, record family property.

places.name: Aila

status.t: end of the Via Nova Traiana

places.summary: Red Sea port at the end of the Via Nova Traiana and base of X Fretensis from c. 300. A mudbrick building there is claimed as the earliest purpose-built church (c. 300).

places.name: Gaza
places.summary: Philistine and Hellenistic trading city at the end of the incense road, famous for its rhetorical school in the 5th-6th centuries; the destruction of its Marneion in 402 is narrated in Mark the Deacon's Life of Porphyry.

places.name: Raphanea
places.summary: Legionary base in the Orontes valley where the soldiers of III Gallica proclaimed the 14-year-old Elagabalus emperor in May 218.

places.name: Zeugma
places.foundedNote: Seleucia on the Euphrates founded c. 300 BC
places.summary: Bridge town on the Euphrates and base of IV Scythica. Rescue excavations before the Birecik dam (2000) uncovered villas with mosaics, including the 'Gypsy girl'.

places.name: Cyrrhus
places.summary: Seleucid city in northern Syria, base of X Fretensis under Augustus and Tiberius, and later the see of the historian-bishop Theodoret (423-c.457).

places.name: Hierapolis Bambyce
places.summary: Sanctuary of the Syrian goddess Atargatis described in Lucian's De Dea Syria; Crassus plundered it in 54-53 BC. Capital of Euphratensis.

places.name: Beroea
places.summary: Seleucid Beroea on the site of Aleppo; Khosrow I burned it in 540 on his way to Antioch, sparing only the citadel.

places.name: Caparcotna
places.foundedNote: fortress of II Traiana then VI Ferrata
places.summary: Fortress of VI Ferrata in the Jezreel valley, whose Latin name Legio survives in Arabic Lajjun; excavated since 2013.

places.name: Betthorus
places.summary: Diocletianic fortress of IV Martia on the Limes Arabicus, the most thoroughly excavated late-Roman legionary base.

places.name: Sergiopolis
places.foundedNote: Diocletianic fort on the Strata Diocletiana
places.summary: Desert fort on the Strata Diocletiana that became the pilgrimage centre of the soldier-martyr Sergius, patron of the Arab tribes; Khosrow II sent votive gifts to the saint.

places.name: Ptolemais
places.summary: Phoenician Akko, refounded by the Ptolemies and made a Claudian veteran colony; base for Vespasian's invasion of Galilee in 67.

places.name: Circesium
places.summary: Fortress fortified by Diocletian at the Khabur mouth, the start of Julian's invasion of Persia in 363 and later a base of IV Parthica.

places.name: Callinicum
places.summary: Euphrates town where Christians burned the synagogue in 388; Ambrose forced Theodosius to withdraw his order of restitution. Belisarius was beaten here by Azarethes on Easter 531.

places.name: Alexandria

status.t: seat of the prefect of Egypt

places.summary: Second city of the empire, capital of the Ptolemies and of Roman Egypt, exporting the grain that fed Rome and later Constantinople. Home of the Museum and Library, of Philo, Origen, Athanasius and Cyril. Caesar was besieged in its palace quarter in 48-47 BC.

places.name: Nicopolis
places.foundedNote: founded on the site of Octavian's victory of 30 BC

status.t: double fortress of III Cyrenaica and XXII Deiotariana

places.summary: Legionary camp 5 km east of Alexandria on the site of Octavian's victory over Antony (1 August 30 BC), garrisoned by the legions of Egypt.

places.name: Pelusium
places.summary: Eastern frontier fortress of Egypt. Pompey was murdered off its beach on 28 September 48 BC; Justinian's plague first appeared here in 541 (Procopius, Wars 2.22).

places.name: Memphis
places.summary: Old capital of Egypt and seat of the Apis cult; Germanicus consulted the Apis bull here in 19, a breach of Augustus's ban on senators entering Egypt.

places.name: Babylon
places.foundedNote: fortress at the head of the Delta

status.t: Diocletianic fortress (legio XIII Gemina in the Notitia)

places.summary: Fortress at the apex of the Delta, rebuilt under Diocletian, whose surrender to Amr ibn al-As in April 641 after a seven-month siege decided the Arab conquest of Egypt. The Hanging Church stands on its gate towers.

places.name: Oxyrhynchus
places.summary: Nome capital whose rubbish mounds, dug by Grenfell and Hunt from 1896, yielded over half a million papyrus fragments: lost Sappho, Menander and Gospel texts beside tax receipts, letters and census returns.

places.name: Antinoopolis
places.summary: City founded by Hadrian where Antinous drowned in the Nile in October 130, with privileges for its Greek citizens; start of the Via Hadriana to the Red Sea.

places.name: Thebae

status.t: Luxor temple converted into a legionary camp

places.summary: Pharaonic capital. Under Diocletian the Luxor temple was enclosed as a camp, and its sanctuary painted with frescoes of the Tetrarchs. Hadrian and Sabina heard the singing Colossus of Memnon in 130.

places.name: Coptos
places.summary: Nile terminus of the desert roads to the Red Sea ports; the Coptos tariff (AD 90) lists tolls, with prostitutes charged 108 drachmas.

places.name: Myos Hormos
places.summary: Red Sea port from which Strabo says 120 ships a year sailed to India under Augustus (2.5.12).

places.name: Berenice
places.foundedNote: founded by Ptolemy II c. 275 BC
places.summary: Southernmost Roman Red Sea port, where excavations found Indian teak, black pepper and a Sanskrit-Prakrit inscription; endpoint of the Via Hadriana.

places.name: Syene
places.summary: Frontier town at the first cataract, where Eratosthenes's measurement of the earth used the noon sun in a well. The Meroites sacked it in 24 BC, prompting Petronius's war.

places.name: Philae
places.summary: Island temple of Isis, the last functioning pagan temple of Egypt, closed by Justinian's general Narses c. 535-537; the latest hieroglyphic inscription (394) is carved here.

places.name: Ammonium
places.summary: Desert oracle of Ammon that hailed Alexander as son of Zeus in 331 BC. Strabo says by his day the oracle was almost deserted (17.1.43); the Romans linked Jupiter Ammon with Egypt's grain and the African legion.

places.name: Mons Claudianus
places.foundedNote: imperial granodiorite quarry, mid-1st to mid-3rd century
places.summary: Imperial quarry of grey granodiorite for the Pantheon portico columns and Trajan's Forum; thousands of ostraca record the rations and water of its workforce.

places.name: Mons Porphyrites
places.foundedNote: quarry of imperial porphyry opened c. 18
places.summary: Sole source of imperial purple porphyry, used for the Tetrarchs statue in Venice and imperial sarcophagi.

places.name: Cyrene

status.t: bequeathed to Rome by Ptolemy Apion

places.summary: Greek city willed to Rome by Ptolemy Apion (96 BC), annexed in 74. The Augustan edicts of Cyrene (7-4 BC) show provincial justice; the Jewish diaspora revolt of 115-117 began here.

places.name: Apollonia
places.summary: Cyrene's harbour, later capital of Libya Pentapolis as Sozusa; much of its port is now submerged.

places.name: Ptolemais
places.summary: Port of Barca refounded by the Ptolemies. Synesius of Cyrene was its bishop (410-413) and complained of Austurian raids.

places.name: Berenice
places.summary: Greek Euesperides refounded as Berenice, modern Benghazi, at the western edge of the Pentapolis.

places.name: Carthago

status.t: Colonia Iulia Concordia Carthago, capital of Africa

places.summary: Rome's great rival, destroyed in 146 BC after a three-year siege, refounded by Caesar and Octavian as capital of Africa and second city of the West. Tertullian, Cyprian and Augustine made it a centre of Latin Christianity; Gaiseric took it on 19 October 439; Belisarius recovered it in 533.

places.name: Utica
places.summary: Phoenician city that deserted Carthage in 149 BC and became the first capital of the province of Africa. Cato the Younger killed himself here in April 46 BC after Thapsus.

places.name: Hadrumetum
places.summary: Phoenician port and capital of Byzacena; its catacombs hold some 15,000 Christian burials. Hannibal landed near here in 203 BC.

places.name: Thapsus
places.summary: Coastal town near which Caesar destroyed the Pompeian army of Metellus Scipio and Juba I on 6 April 46 BC; his veterans massacred 10,000 surrendering men.

places.name: Leptis Magna
places.summary: Phoenician city whose olive wealth paid an annual fine of 3 million pounds of oil to Caesar. Birthplace of Septimius Severus, who rebuilt it with a new forum, basilica and harbour; buried by sand, it is one of the best preserved Roman cities.

places.name: Oea
places.summary: Phoenician port, one of the three cities of Tripolitania. Apuleius married the widow Pudentilla here and was tried for magic at Sabratha (c. 158), defending himself in the Apology. The arch of Marcus Aurelius (163) survives.

places.name: Sabratha
places.summary: Tripolitanian port with a three-storey theatre stage restored in the 1930s; Apuleius's magic trial was heard here.

places.name: Cirta
places.summary: Numidian royal capital on its gorge. Jugurtha's massacre of the Italian traders after its fall in 112 BC provoked Rome's war; Sittius's mercenaries received it in 46 BC. Rebuilt by Constantine after Maxentius's troops destroyed it in 311.

places.name: Hippo Regius
places.summary: Port where Augustine was bishop from 396 until his death on 28 August 430 in the third month of the Vandal siege.

places.name: Thugga
places.summary: Hill town with a bilingual Libyco-Punic royal mausoleum and a Capitolium of 166-167; a double community of Numidian civitas and Roman pagus until united in 205.

places.name: Zama Regia

status.t: Juba I's capital, shut its gates to him

places.summary: Numidian town that gave its name to Scipio's defeat of Hannibal in 202 BC, though the battlefield (perhaps near Naraggara) is uncertain; inscriptions place Zama Regia at Jama.

places.name: Sufetula
places.summary: Town with three temples of the Capitoline triad; the rebel exarch Gregory made it his capital and was killed near it by the Arab army in 647.

places.name: Thysdrus
places.summary: Olive town where landowners killed the procurator and proclaimed Gordian I emperor in 238. Its amphitheatre for 35,000 is the third largest in the Roman world.

places.name: Lambaesis
places.foundedNote: fortress of III Augusta from c. 115
places.summary: Fortress of III Augusta, whose praetorium and parade ground with Hadrian's adlocutio (128) survive in the Aurès foothills.

places.name: Theveste
places.summary: Base of III Augusta (c. 75-115), then a colony at the head of Hadrian's road from Carthage; Solomon rebuilt its walls in 535.

places.name: Ammaedara
places.summary: First base of III Augusta, refounded as a Flavian veteran colony when the legion moved west; a large Byzantine fort was built here.

places.name: Thamugadi
places.foundedNote: Colonia Marciana Ulpia Traiana Thamugadi, AD 100, by III Augusta for veterans
places.summary: Trajan's veteran colony, a near-perfect grid of 12 ha built by III Augusta; an inscription in its forum reads 'venari lavari ludere ridere occ est vivere' (to hunt, bathe, play and laugh, that is life).

places.name: Cuicul
places.summary: Nervan colony on a mountain spur with a Severan forum and an exceptionally well preserved urban layout.

places.name: Sitifis
places.summary: Colony that became capital of Diocletian's Mauretania Sitifensis.

places.name: Caesarea

status.t: capital of Juba II and Cleopatra Selene
capital of Mauretania Caesariensis, colonia Claudia

places.summary: Juba II's capital, renamed for Augustus, with a court library and Greek sculptures; Caligula's murder of King Ptolemy in 40 led to annexation. Base of a fleet squadron.

places.name: Tingis
places.summary: Capital of Mauretania Tingitana facing Spain, administratively joined to the Spanish diocese after Diocletian. The centurion Marcellus was martyred here in 298.

places.name: Volubilis
places.summary: Mauretanian city rewarded by Claudius with citizenship and municipal status after its loyalty in the revolt of Aedemon. Rome withdrew c. 285, but Latin inscriptions continue to 655.

places.name: Lixus
places.summary: Phoenician town said by Pliny to be the oldest in the West, linked to the Garden of the Hesperides; garum factories line its port.

places.name: Sala
places.summary: Southernmost Roman town on the Atlantic, protected by a ditch and wall; an inscription of 144 honours the prefect M. Sulpicius Felix for defending it from raiders.

places.name: Tipasa
places.summary: Coastal colony near the Royal Mausoleum of Mauretania; Victor of Vita says Huneric cut out the tongues of its Catholics in 484.

places.name: Bulla Regia
places.summary: Numidian town whose villas have underground storeys to escape the summer heat, with mosaics in place.

places.name: Capsa
places.summary: Oasis town that Marius took by a desert march in 107 BC, killing the men and selling the rest despite its surrender (Sallust, Jug. 89-91).
